extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, journalists, human rights advocates, and the general public concerned with freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: A Human Rights Watch question-and-answer guidance explaining how international human rights law constrains governments' ability to censor offensive speech, using the Danish cartoons controversy as the focal case. It lays out legal standards, exceptions, and policy recommendations for states, editors, and civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments may not suppress speech merely because it is offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Rights Watch affirms that, under the right of freedom of expression, governments are not entitled to suppress speech simply because it is offensive or disrespectful of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although governments may personally deplore or disapprove of speech, international human rights law speaks to whether governments must permit such speech, not whether it was wise or proper to publish it. Officials can clarify that content does not reflect official views or express that using freedom of expression in that way was unwise, but they should not impose censorship on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on freedom of expression must be interpreted narrowly
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom to express controversial points of view is necessary for democratic accountability; limitations imposed by human rights law must be strictly necessary and interpreted narrowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because permitting censorship of provocative or offensive speech risks empowering officials to silence criticism of them, restrictions should be the exception. Courts and governments should require a high threshold of necessity before restricting speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate speech/incitement standard: only imminent incitement to unlawful acts can be suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy of religious hatred can be suppressed only when it constitutes imminent incitement to unlawful acts of discrimination, hostility or violence, and when the speech actually urges or promotes such acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech that targets a religion for disrespect, as opposed to speech that targets believers for unlawful acts, is protected even if offensive. It is not incitement when opponents of speech use violence—that cannot be used to justify censorship. Authorities must show that the speech urged or promoted imminent unlawful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between targeting religion and targeting believers for unlawful acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that disparages a religion (disrespect toward beliefs) is different from speech that advocates unlawful acts against believers; only the latter (when it meets the incitement test) may be restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and enforcement should focus on whether speech promotes discrimination, hostility, or violence against persons or groups, not merely whether it offends doctrinal sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public safety exception requires strict necessity in a democratic society
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of expression may be limited to protect public safety and the rights of others, but such limitations must be strictly 'necessary' in a democratic society; banning provocative speech rarely meets that test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats of violence by protesters should be contained through law enforcement; governments tolerating unlawful protest behavior cannot blame the original speech. Wherever possible, meet offensive speech with counter-speech rather than censorship in the name of public safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of religion does not create a right to censor others
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious freedom means liberty to adopt beliefs and live according to them, but it does not give anyone the right to impose religious beliefs on others or to insist that others abide by those views through censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious objections can be stated and politically pressed, but they do not translate into legal entitlement to ban or censor expressions that others lawfully publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments have higher responsibilities in speech matters
rubrics_metrics.description: While government officials enjoy free-speech rights, they also have a parallel responsibility, beyond that of ordinary citizens, to protect welfare, lives and rights of their people, and to combat discrimination and intolerance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these duties, governments should be especially careful not to speak in ways that encourage violence, discrimination or hatred, and should reaffirm obligations to maintain a peaceful, open and tolerant society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility vs. state censorship: accountability should be non-state
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should be held responsible for publication choices by their readers, communities, or employers, not by their governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under freedom of expression, governments cannot impose views of what is fit to publish except in very limited cases (e.g., proven incitement). Editors may face social, commercial, or professional consequences for poor editorial judgment, but not state punishment where speech is protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for republishers from state retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Republishers of material that is protected should enjoy the same protection from state retaliation as the original publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where editorial judgment in republishing is questioned (for example, in a volatile global context), international human rights law still protects republication from governmental punishment unless the material meets a valid restriction test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peaceful protest is protected and governments must facilitate and protect it
rubrics_metrics.description: Human rights law protects the right to peacefully protest offensive speech; governments have a duty to make peaceful protest possible and to protect the public from protests that turn violent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities should enable assembly, protect life and property during protests, take action against specific threats, and avoid discriminatory speech/actions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-speech and positive measures are preferable to censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectionable speech is best met with contrary speech, not censorship; governments can counter offensive speech by fulfilling obligations to protect minorities and by making clear they reject discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities and civil society should denounce offensive content, promote public debate, and take positive steps to protect vulnerable communities rather than seek bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws banning certain speech (e.g., Holocaust denial) risk disproportionate restrictions and double standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting speech such as Holocaust denial may have been motivated by historical context and survivor protection, but such laws disproportionately restrict freedom of expression and create questions of discriminatory application when applied unevenly across religions or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human Rights Watch argues these laws should be reconsidered because they can be counterproductive (making extremists martyrs) and because differential legal treatment of offensive speech raises legitimacy concerns; equal protection and freedom of speech should be mutually reinforcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violent responses to speech do not justify censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not justification for censorship that opponents of speech respond with violence; allowing violent opposition to determine what is censored grants censorship power to those willing to use force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should instead suppress unlawful violent conduct and protect speech rights; tolerating protesters' violence undermines the rule of law and cannot be used as grounds to ban the initial expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of international human rights law in assessing publication decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: International human rights law obliges governments to protect religious freedom and minorities but primarily concerns what governments must permit rather than endorsing or condemning particular publications; it cannot dictate whether publication was wise or proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human rights law provides the legal framework for state action (or restraint) but leaves moral, editorial, and political judgments about publication to public debate, press institutions, and civil society.
